title: Young woman with Guillain‐Barré syndrome and cervical transverse myelitis—A new GBS variant, not coincidence
case_prompt:
A 40-year-old previously healthy obese woman noted lower extremity numbness and tingling 4 days before admission, with no weakness until 1 day prior. One week earlier, she had developed left facial weakness diagnosed as Bell’s palsy. She denied recent illness or vaccination. On admission, temperature was 99.2 °F, blood pressure 167/78 mm Hg, and other vitals were normal. Examination showed left lower facial weakness involving the forehead, motor strength 4/5 in the upper extremities and 3/5 in the lower extremities, absent deep tendon reflexes, negative Hoffmann sign, and decreased light-touch and cold sensation below C5 bilaterally; extraocular movements were intact, and nystagmus was absent. There was no bowel or bladder involvement; mentation was normal.  
On hospital day 2, strength declined to 2/5 in all extremities with still absent reflexes. She developed bilateral ptosis, urinary incontinence, and early respiratory failure. On day 3, ptosis worsened, she developed ophthalmoplegia and prominent nystagmus (upbeat on up-gaze, downbeat on down-gaze), and required intubation.  
Laboratory studies showed WBC 15.6 × 10^3/µL on admission (nadir 9.0), normal chemistry, vitamin B12 1324 pg/mL, TSH 2.6 µIU/mL, HbA1c 5.7%, and negative aquaporin-4 antibody, HIV, and various infectious CSF titers. CSF analysis revealed 0 WBCs, 1 RBC, protein 114 mg/dL, glucose 72 mg/dL. MRI of the head was normal. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated an ill-defined T2 hyperintense signal within the cord extending to and likely above the cervicomedullary junction.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Isolated cervicomedullary junction lesion — “A cervicomedullary junction lesion would not present with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia as did this patient.”  
2. Miller Fisher variant — “The case presented above is not consistent with the Miller Fisher variant due to minimal extraocular movement issues aside from prominent vertical nystagmus, and maintenance of full sensory response.”  
3. Bickerstaff’s brainstem encephalitis — “The patient had no encephalopathy ... further imaging findings on MRI were not consistent with significant brain stem involvement and the patient maintained full preservation of mental status.”  
4. Pharyngeal–cervical–brachial variant — “The patient did not fit the clinical picture for the pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant because the cranial nerves were involved and she was quadriplegic as well as had findings of myelitis on MRI.”  
5. MFv–BBE crossover — “Due to the patient’s presentation of classic ascending GBS and cervical spine myelitis on MRI, a crossover of Miller Fisher and BBE was excluded as a diagnosis.”  
6. Transverse myelitis alone — while MRI and sensory level support TM, “A cervicomedullary junction lesion would not present with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia” and the albuminocytologic dissociation and areflexia point toward GBS.
